[0:08] that this is all about ancient religious hatreds.
[0:10] In fact, while religion is involved, the conflict is mostly about two groups of people who claim
[0:15] the same land.
[0:16] And it really only goes back about a century, to the early 1900s.
[0:19] Around then, the region along the eastern Mediterranean we now call
[0:24] Israel-Palestine had been under Ottoman rule for centuries.
[0:27] It was religiously diverse, including mostly Muslims and Christians but also a small number
[0:31] of Jews, who lived generally in peace.
[0:33] And it was changing in two important ways.
[0:36] First, more people in the region were developing a sense of being not just ethnic Arabs
[0:40] but Palestinians, a distinct national identity.
[0:43] At the same time, not so far away in Europe, more Jews were joining a movement called Zionism,
[0:49] which said that Judaism was not just a religion but a nationality, one that deserved a nation
[0:54] of its own.
[0:55] And after centuries of persecution, many believed a Jewish state was their only way of
[0:59] safety.
[1:00] And they saw their historic homeland in the Middle East as their best hope for establishing it.
[1:05] In the first decades of the 20th century, tens of thousands of European Jews moved there.
[1:10] After World War One, the Ottoman Empire collapsed, and the British and French Empires carved
[1:16] up the Middle East, with the British taking control of a region it called the British
[1:19] Mandate for Palestine.
[1:22] At first, the British allowed Jewish immigration.
[1:26] But as more Jews arrived, settling into farming communes, tension between Jews and Arabs grew.
[1:32] Both sides committed acts of violence.
[1:34] And by the 1930s, the British began limiting Jewish immigration.  In response,  Jewish militias
[1:40] formed to fight both the local Arabs and to resist British rule.
[1:44] Then came the Holocaust, leading many more Jews to flee Europe for British Palestine,
[1:49] and galvanizing much of the world in support of a Jewish state.
[1:53] In 1947, as sectarian violence between Arabs and Jews there grew,
[1:57] the United Nations approved a plan to divide British Palestine into two separate states:
[2:02] one for Jews, Israel, and one for Arabs, Palestine.
[2:06] The city of Jerusalem, where Jews, Muslims, and Christians

[2:12] The plan was meant to give Jews a state, to establish Palestinian independence, and to
[2:18] end the sectarian violence that the British could no longer control.
[2:21] The Jews accepted the plan and declared independence as Israel.
[2:25] But Arabs throughout the region saw the UN plan as just more European colonialism trying to steal their land.
[2:32] Many of the Arab states, who had just recently won independence themselves, declared war on Israel
